newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIA RUGBY LEAGUE COMPS SAY PEACE DEAL CLOSER.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIA RUGBY LEAGUE COMPS SAY PEACE DEAL CLOSER.

text.p: Australia's two warring rugby league competitions, who are estimated to have spent over A$500 million of their pay television backers' money fighting each other, said on Thursday they were a step closer to a peace deal.

The Australian Rugby League (ARL), funded by pay television and telecommunications group Optus Communications, met with the News Corp -funded Super League right through Wednesday and both issued statements saying a deal was closer.
"The ARL and News Ltd today considered an ARL proposal for a united and fully integrated competition in 1998," the ARL said in a statement issued early on Thursday.
"The meeting was the most productive held between the two organisations," the ARL said.
Super League confirmed the ARL had put forward a proposal for a united competition and that this had been discussed at length and amended.
"The amended proposal will now be put to the ARL and the NSWRL (New South Wales Rugby League) boards and the Super League clubs," Super League said in a statement.
"The meeting today was a genuinely positive step towards a unified game in 1998," News Director of Sport Ian Frykberg said in the statement.
ARL chief executive Neil Whittaker also said a number of issues had to be referred back to the 22 clubs currently in both competitions.
"There are some very positive things for us to consider," Whittaker said.
"Both sides have agreed to act quickly in these discussions," he said.

Early this year, News launched a separate rugby league competition to provide sports programming for Foxtel, the joint venture cable pay television joint venture it has with the government-owned Telstra Corp AOT.AX.

News is believed to have committed about A$400 million to set up and run the rebel league in Australia and the established leagues in New Zealand, Britain and France with which Super League is aligned.

The established ARL, which fought News' attempt to set up Super League, is backed by Foxtel-competitor Optus Vision, which was recently fully merged with Optus Communications, Telstra's main competitor.
Optus is thought to have spent about A$120 million funding the 12 ARL clubs in the main competition and the ARL itself.

But earlier this year a peace deal between News' Excecutive Chairman Rupert Murdoch and ARL-aligned media mogul Kerry Packer, along with poor crowds and television ratings, sparked talks to bring the two competitions together.

News, Telstra, Optus and other pay television players have also baulked at the mounting losses generated in the battle to set up cable pay television in Australia, forcing an industry rationalisation.
Over A$1 billion is estimated to have been lost by cable and satellite pay television operators in the four years since pay television started in Australia.
The main satellite pay television operator, Australis Media Ltd, has agreed to merger with Foxtel.
